title: Cattle Creek Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Cattle Creek wells have a 130 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $12,500-$21,800.
h1: Cattle Creek Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
For rural property near Cattle Creek, the local well records point to moderate drilling depths but variable ground conditions. Among permitted wells within five miles, the median total depth is 130 feet, and the median reported pump yield is 15 gallons per minute.

Those figures are useful for early budgeting, not a guarantee for a particular lot. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, so nearby results can help but do not eliminate uncertainty. Check the permit record, construction report, water rights, and neighboring wells before you commit to a property or a drilling contract.

sections.heading: Cattle Creek Well Depth: What the Ground Requires
sections.html:
Recorded well depths near Cattle Creek vary considerably. The median is 130 feet, with the middle half between 71 and 240 feet. About 38% of wells are under 100 feet, while 43% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 17% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 2% exceed 600 feet.

The deepest recorded well is 3,190 feet, but that is not a normal bidding assumption. The local aquifer records are dominated by unnamed or fractured-bedrock wells, with a smaller number of alluvial and Mancos wells. For a driller's estimate, use the middle-half range as the starting planning window and ask what nearby wells actually encountered.

sections.heading: Expected Well Yield Around Cattle Creek
sections.html:
Reported production is generally stronger than the depth variation. The median pump yield is 15 gallons per minute, and the middle half of reported yields runs from 12 to 15 gallons per minute. About 71% of wells report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 27% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

Only 3% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and none are recorded under 1 gallon per minute. That is encouraging for ordinary household use, but the yield sample is smaller than the depth sample: 476 wells report a pump yield. A well test, storage-tank plan, and intended use still matter, especially if irrigation or livestock is part of the property plan.

sections.heading: Water Levels and the Cattle Creek Trend
sections.html:
The recorded median static water level is 71 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 30 and 164 feet. This is the standing water level measured in the well, not the depth drilled. A shallow static level can reduce pumping lift, but the water level can vary by location, season, well construction, and measurement date.

The decade series does not show a simple uninterrupted decline. Median depth to water was 32 feet in the 1980s, 105 feet in the 1990s, and 150 feet in the 2010s, then 64 feet in the 2020s. That rebound means the records alone do not establish a steadily dropping water table. Get current measurements for the specific parcel.

sections.heading: Who Has Drilled Near Cattle Creek, and When
sections.html:
The permit history is broad, with 2,043 wells in the Colorado DWR records for the mapped area. Of those, 988 are recorded as constructed, 1,230 report a total depth, and 476 report a pump yield. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently listed drillers are Shelton Drilling Corporation, with 656 records; Collins Drilling Co, with 233; and Mountain Drilling Co., with 140. The permit count is highest in the 1990s, at 542, followed by the 2000s with 323. Treat those names as a record-history reference, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, availability, scope, and insurance before hiring.

sections.heading: Cattle Creek Well Drilling Cost and Budget
sections.html:
The cost model for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 130 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $6,500 to $9,800. That is only the hole and should not be mistaken for a complete water system.

A finished well including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,500 to $21,800 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, longer utility runs, or unusual ground can move the final bid. Ask each driller to separate drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, testing, trenching, electrical, and any permit-related work.

sections.heading: Risks to Check Before Building Near Cattle Creek
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main signal in these records, but a strong area median does not protect every lot. Fractured bedrock can produce uneven results, including a dry hole or a well that meets a drilling target but does not support the planned use. Verify neighboring construction reports rather than relying on a single nearby well.

Environmental due diligence also matters. Within about ten miles, the map includes 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 23 historic mine features. There are no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites listed in the facts, but that does not replace a water-quality test. Test for appropriate contaminants, confirm septic setbacks and soil conditions, and make sure the well location works with the house, access, drainfield, and future additions.

sections.heading: Buying or Building on a Cattle Creek Lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's well permit and the construction reports for nearby properties in Cattle Creek, Carbondale, Mulford, No Name, Glenwood Springs, Catherine, and El Jebel. Compare depth, static water level, yield, casing, grout, and reported use. Most local permits are for domestic or household use, at 67% of the records; irrigation accounts for 6%, stock for 4%, and monitoring for 15%.

Before closing, make the well and septic evaluation a defined contingency. Confirm the permitted use, test the water, obtain a current flow or recovery test, and price the complete connection to the proposed building site. If you plan more than ordinary household use, review water-rights requirements and any need for an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin. A DWR permit is not the same as a guaranteed water supply.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Cattle Creek?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within five miles of Cattle Creek is 130 feet. The middle half runs from 71 to 240 feet. About 38% are under 100 feet, while 43% are between 100 and 300 feet. The records also include much deeper wells, so a nearby construction report is more useful than the median alone for a specific lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Cattle Creek?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 130-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,500 to $9,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,500 to $21,800. Difficult access, deeper drilling, casing, grout, and longer utility runs can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Cattle Creek wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 15 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 12 and 15 gallons per minute. About 71% of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute, while 3% produce between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. These results come from 476 yield reports, so test the specific well before relying on the area figures.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Cattle Creek?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water is safe to drink. Testing is important because the mapped area includes 19 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 23 historic mine features within about ten miles. Test the actual well for appropriate contaminants, review its construction report, and use qualified water-quality guidance before making it a household supply.

faq.q: Are Cattle Creek wells running dry?
faq.a: The available water-level series does not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 32 feet in the 1980s, 105 feet in the 1990s, 150 feet in the 2010s, and 64 feet in the 2020s. Individual wells can differ sharply, especially in fractured bedrock. Ask for current static-level, pumping, and recovery information for the property.
